THOUGHT: The clinical picture is a chronic, progressively firm, bilateral periocular/eyelid pseudotumoral process with lacrimal gland involvement. Key diagnostic data strongly point to IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD): markedly elevated serum IgG4 (202.5 mg/dL), an IgG4+/IgG+ plasma cell ratio >60%, 116 IgG4+ plasma cells/HPF, storiform fibrosis, dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with many plasma cells and eosinophils, and elevated total IgE and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. These histopathologic features meet accepted criteria for IgG4-RD (dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, storiform fibrosis, high IgG4+ cell count and ratio); obliterative phlebitis can be absent and its absence does not exclude the diagnosis. Imaging limited to the orbit and negative systemic PET/CT is compatible with localized IgG4-related ophthalmic disease. Alternative diagnoses that can mimic this presentation include orbital lymphoma (especially MALT/marginal zone lymphoma), idiopathic orbital inflammation (orbital pseudotumor), Kimura disease, and granulomatous conditions such as sarcoidosis or ANCA-associated vasculitis — these are less likely given the specific histology and serology, but remain considerations until clonality and other specific studies are definitively excluded.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. IgG4-related orbital disease (IgG4-related dacryoadenitis / orbital pseudotumor) — most likely
2. Extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma of the orbit/lacrimal gland — important mimic to exclude
3. Idiopathic orbital inflammation (nonspecific orbital pseudotumor) — less likely given IgG4 findings
4. Kimura disease (eosinophilic lymphoid hyperplasia) — considered because of high IgE and eosinophils but histology favors IgG4-RD
5. Sarcoidosis / other granulomatous orbital disease or ANCA-associated orbital vasculitis — less likely given negative systemic workup and lacking granulomas or typical vasculitic features
ground_truth: Eosinophilic angiocentric sclerosis related to IgG4 with isolated eyelid involvement
